contentReview.note: Life-application and belonging content drafted by Claude after a planning discussion with Pastor Eric. It must be approved by Pastor Eric or the designated lead teacher before children see it. Read the whole lesson in preview mode (the play page without a child selected) and check: (1) the names and situations ring true for our children, (2) nothing could single out a real child, (3) the Bible is used faithfully.

names.note: Names used in the life-application scenarios. Characters ALTERNATE between the two lists (a non-African name, then an African one, then a non-African one...), in the order they appear in the lesson, so no lesson reads as all one heritage. The app never uses a child's own name for a character. African day-names are Ghanaian (Akan); Tunde and Emeka are Nigerian (Yoruba and Igbo). Edit freely to match your congregation; list only names you are happy to see in any role.

character.name: David
character.trait: trusting God when things look big

translation.name: World English Bible
translation.note: WEB renders God's name as "Yahweh". A church that prefers "the LORD" needs a display setting; not built yet.

ageNotes.explorer: Keep to two ideas: God chose David because of his heart, and God helped David be brave.
ageNotes.trailblazer: Add the lion and the bear (17:34-37), Saul's armour (17:38-39) and David's words to Goliath (17:45).

bigIdea: God looks at the heart, and God helps us be brave.

sensitivity.notes: Goliath is killed (17:49-50). For Explorers say the giant fell down and God's people were safe; do not dwell on it. If a child asks directly, answer honestly and briefly: the giant died, and God's people were safe. Trailblazers can hear the account as written.

preClass.teaser: Somebody in this story was the youngest in his family, and nobody thought he'd matter. Can you work out who?

clues: I was the youngest in my family.
I spent my days looking after sheep.
God chose me, even though nobody else expected it.
I faced a giant with a sling.

roles.storyteller: Tells the story. The only voice for the main narrative.
roles.coFacilitator: Runs chat and reactions, admits children from the waiting room, watches for anyone lost or upset.

part1.title: The shepherd boy
part1.retelling: God sent the prophet Samuel to a man called Jesse in Bethlehem, because God had chosen one of Jesse's sons to be the next king. Jesse's sons walked past one by one. They looked tall and strong, and Samuel thought, surely it's him. But God said no. Then Samuel asked, "Are all your children here?" There was one more: the youngest, out looking after the sheep. His name was David. They sent for him. God said, "This is the one." Samuel poured oil on David's head, and God's Spirit came on David from that day on.

quoted.text: But Yahweh said to Samuel, “Don’t look on his face, or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; for I don’t see as man sees. For man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart.”

part1.prop: A shepherd's staff (or a walking stick).

part2.title: The giant
part2.retelling: Israel's army was camped on one hill and their enemies, the Philistines, on another. Every day a giant named Goliath walked out and shouted a challenge, and everyone in Israel's army was afraid. David had been sent by his father with food for his brothers, and he heard the giant. David said, "I'll go." King Saul said David was too young, but David told him how God had helped him against a lion and a bear while he looked after his sheep. Saul gave David his own armour, but it was too heavy and David took it off. David picked up his shepherd's staff, chose five smooth stones from the stream, and took his sling. He told Goliath he was coming in the name of the God of Israel. Then he ran towards the giant, put a stone in his sling, and the stone struck Goliath, who fell to the ground.
part2.explorerVersion: Everyone was scared of a giant called Goliath. But David wasn't. David remembered how God had helped him before, when he looked after his sheep. So David took his sling and five smooth stones. He didn't wear armour and he didn't have a sword. God helped David, and the giant fell down. God's people were safe.

quoted.text: David said, “Yahweh who delivered me out of the paw of the lion, and out of the paw of the bear, he will deliver me out of the hand of this Philistine.”

Then David said to the Philistine, “You come to me with a sword, with a spear, and with a javelin; but I come to you in the name of Yahweh of Armies, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied.

part2.prop: A sling (or a rolled-up sock), and one smooth stone.

activities.prompt: Everyone stand up. When the leader says "sheep", crouch and go "baa". When the leader says "shepherd", stand tall and hold out a staff. Swap a few times, going faster.
Would you have gone out to face the giant? Show thumbs up, thumbs down, or a wobbly thumb. No wrong answers.
The leader answers as David while the children ask questions.

activities.prompt: Find 1 Samuel 17:37 in your own Bible, or follow along on the leader's screen. Who does David say helped him before?

Open questions, no single right answer. Don't rush to a moral.
questions: I wonder which part of the story you liked best.

I wonder where you are in this story.

options: It didn't fit him and was too heavy

trailblazer.q: Finish the verse: "Man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the ..."

actions: Point to your eyes for "outward appearance"
Hand on your heart for "looks at the heart"

apply.intro: Life questions placed where the story meets a child's week. LIVE: the leader asks them aloud and lets children answer in their own words. APP: the same moment is a tap on a choice that ends by handing the conversation to a grown-up. Nothing a child taps is stored, and no choice is 'wrong'. Every choice gets a kind, honest reply.
apply.howToUse: Leaders: read the scenario, ask the question, let two or three children answer, then give the Bible's answer. Never ask a child to speak for their culture or family. If a child says something that worries you, follow the leaders' safeguarding checklist. Names come from the pool in "names"; swap in names that are not in your group, especially for the child who is left out or laughed at.

moments.title: Left out at break
moments.scenario: {boy1} is the smallest boy in his class. When teams are picked for football at break, {boy1} is picked last. Again.
moments.question: When God looks at {boy1}, what does God see?

choices.text: A boy who is too small
choices.response: That is what eyes see on the outside. But God looks at the heart, and God sees a boy he made and loves.

choices.text: A boy God made and loves
choices.response: Yes! God saw David's heart, not how big he was. God sees {boy1}'s heart too.

choices.text: I'm not sure
choices.response: That's okay. Let's wonder together: God looked at David's heart instead of his size. What might God see when he looks at {boy1}?

moments.grownUpTalk: Ask a grown-up: Was there ever a time you felt left out? What helped?
moments.leaderPrompt: Ask everyone: "Have you ever seen someone picked last? How do you think they felt?" Let two or three children answer, then ask: "What does God see when he looks at him?" Don't push for a 'right' answer; come back to 1 Samuel 16:7.

moments.title: A wobbly tummy
moments.scenario: {girl1} has to read out loud in front of her whole class. Her tummy feels wobbly, and she thinks she might get it wrong. It feels like a giant.
moments.question: David remembered how God had helped him before. What could {girl1} do?

choices.text: Take a deep breath and tell God she feels scared
choices.response: Yes! David trusted God, and we can tell God about our wobbly feelings. He is always listening.

choices.text: Remember a time God helped her before
choices.response: Great idea! David remembered the lion and the bear. What could {girl1} remember?

choices.text: Tell a friend or her teacher she feels nervous
choices.response: That is brave too! God gives us people to help us, like a smooth stone in David's bag.

moments.grownUpTalk: Ask a grown-up: What is a wobbly-tummy giant you have faced? How did God help you?
moments.leaderPrompt: Ask: "Who has ever felt wobbly before doing something scary?" Then: "What did David remember?" (the lion and the bear, 17:37). "What could you remember about how God has helped you?" Let children answer; nobody has to.

moments.title: The new girl at lunch
moments.scenario: {girl2}'s family has just moved to a new town. On her first day at school, nobody knows her, and she sits all on her own at lunch.
moments.question: God sees {girl2}'s heart. What could you do if you saw someone new sitting alone?

choices.text: Sit with her and say hello
choices.response: Yes! That is what God's love looks like when it has hands and feet. Now she is not alone.

choices.text: Ask her to play with us
choices.response: A great way to help someone feel like they belong!

choices.text: Tell a grown-up she might need a friend
choices.response: Also kind! A grown-up can help, and you can still say hello too.

moments.grownUpTalk: Ask a grown-up: Do you remember being new somewhere? What did someone do that helped?

moments.title: When could I use this verse?
moments.scenario: You have learned: "God looks at the heart." A verse is for using, not just for remembering.
moments.question: When could you say it quietly to yourself?

choices.text: When I feel left out
choices.response: Good choice. Say it, take a breath, and remember: God sees your heart. Then maybe ask someone to play.

choices.text: When I feel small
choices.response: Good choice. God looked at David's heart when he was the smallest in his family. He sees yours too.

choices.text: When someone says something unkind
choices.response: Good choice. What they say is not the whole story of you. God looks at the heart. If it keeps happening, tell a grown-up.

moments.grownUpTalk: Try saying the verse together at bedtime this week.

moments.title: A name that's hard to say
moments.scenario: {girl1} has just started at a new school. Some kids laugh at how her name sounds, and one of them says, "Can I just call you something easier?" {girl1} wonders whether she should change who she is to fit in.
moments.question: People looked at David's outside and missed his heart. What does it mean that God looks at {girl1}'s heart?

choices.text: God knows her real name and who she is, even when others get it wrong
choices.response: Yes. Her name is not a problem to fix. Later in this study we will see what God says about names.

choices.text: She should quietly change her name so the laughing stops
choices.response: A lot of people have felt that pressure, and it is understandable. But God is not embarrassed by her name, and she does not have to hide it. There are braver, kinder ways. And if others keep being unkind, a teacher should know.

choices.text: She could kindly teach them to say it right, and ask a teacher for help if it doesn't stop
choices.response: That takes courage. Nobody should have to handle unkindness alone. Telling a teacher is not weak. It is wise.

moments.grownUpTalk: Ask a grown-up: Do you know how your name was chosen? Has anyone ever got your name wrong?
moments.leaderPrompt: Ask: "Has anyone ever had their name said wrong, or been teased about it? You don't have to share." Then: "What does God see when he looks at her?" Never ask a child to explain their name, culture or family to the group. Move on gently if nobody wants to answer.

moments.title: The pressure to join in
moments.scenario: {boy1} is in a class group chat. Some older kids start sending mean jokes about {boy2}, who is new, and everyone is replying with laughing emojis. {boy1}'s stomach twists. Joining in would be easy.
moments.question: Some giants are not big men with spears. They are the pressure to go along with the crowd. What could a David-heart do?

choices.text: Not join in, and stay quiet
choices.response: Not joining in matters. But staying quiet can feel lonely, and {boy2} may still be hurting. There is more he could do.

choices.text: Send {boy2} a kind message on his own
choices.response: Kindness costs something, and it can change someone's whole day.

choices.text: Tell a grown-up he trusts about the chat
choices.response: That is brave, not telling tales. Mean messages online are something grown-ups need to know about.

moments.grownUpTalk: Ask a grown-up: What would you want a friend to do if people were being unkind about you online? What should we do as a family if something like this happens?
moments.leaderPrompt: Ask: "What makes it hard to go against the group?" Then: "What is one small stone you have?" (prayer, a friend, a trusted adult, remembering what God has done). Affirm telling a trusted adult as courage. If a child says they are being bullied, follow the leaders' safeguarding checklist.

moments.title: More than a mark
moments.scenario: {boy3} got a low mark in a maths test. A friend says, "Guess you're just not clever." {boy3} is starting to believe it.
moments.question: Is one test mark the same as who {boy3} is? What does God look at?

choices.text: God looks at his heart, and one mark doesn't say who he is
choices.response: Yes. A mark tells you what to practise. It does not tell you who you are.

choices.text: The mark shows he should try again, and ask for help
choices.response: Wise. Asking for help is what brave people do. David did not face the giant alone in his own strength.

choices.text: Maybe he should give up on maths
choices.response: Lots of people feel like that after a bad mark. Take a rest, then ask someone who can help. God cares about {boy3}'s heart and his effort, not just the mark.

moments.grownUpTalk: Ask a grown-up: Was there ever something you were told you weren't good at? What happened?

moments.title: When could I use this verse?
moments.scenario: A memory verse is a tool, not a trophy. "Man looks at the outward appearance, but Yahweh looks at the heart."
moments.question: When might you need it this week?

choices.text: When someone laughs at how I look or sound
choices.response: Say it in your head. What they see is not the whole of you. If it keeps happening, tell a grown-up you trust.

choices.text: When I feel too small or too different
choices.response: David was the youngest and the one nobody thought of. God chose him because he looked at his heart.

choices.text: When I'm tempted to join in being unkind
choices.response: That is a giant-sized moment. Say the verse, remember whose heart you want to have, and take one brave step the other way.

choices.text: When I have made a mistake and feel not good enough
choices.response: One mistake is not who you are. God looks at the heart, and he is kind to people who come to him.

moments.grownUpTalk: Pick one moment this week when you will say the verse, and tell a grown-up which one.

spotlight.why: A woman from a different land who chose to follow the God of Israel, and became David's great-grandmother.

belonging.intro: Every lesson in this series asks one question: who else is in this story? The Bible is not one family's history. It is God's invitation to every family, and this is how it begins to show in David's own family line.
belonging.leaderPrompt: Tell it simply: Ruth was not born in Israel, and she chose God's people. Ask: "Did you know David's great-grandmother came from a different country?" Then read the promise and the name verse together. Do not ask individual children to say where their family is from; let anyone share if they want to.

cards.title: Ruth: from far away, in God's family
cards.text: David's great-grandmother was called Ruth. She was not born in Israel. She came from a different land, called Moab, and she chose to follow the God of Israel. Ruth's family became David's family.

quote.text: They named him Obed. He is the father of Jesse, the father of David.

cards.title: God's promise for every family
cards.text: Long before David, God made a promise. It was for people from every family on earth. That blessing came through Jesus, who was born in David's family line. So families from Ghana, Nigeria, Jamaica, England, India and everywhere else are invited in.

quote.text: All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.

cards.title: God knows your name
cards.text: God does not mix up names. Whether you are called Jason or Kweku, Sophie or Adjoa, Alfie or Kojo, Chloe or Ama, Joe or Emeka, Molly or Tunde, or any other name from anywhere in the world, God says this to his people:

quote.text: I have called you by your name. You are mine.

cards.title: Every nation, tribe and language
cards.text: The Bible ends with a picture of people from everywhere, standing together to worship God.

quote.text: a great multitude, which no man could count, out of every nation and of all tribes, peoples, and languages

parentEmail.note: Used in the short email a parent receives after their child attends a live class. {child} becomes the child's first name. Keep the synopsis to two or three sentences and do not give away how the story ends for younger children. Reviewed with the rest of the lesson.
parentEmail.synopsis: David was the youngest son in his family, and he looked after his father's sheep. God chose him to be king because God looks at the heart, not at how big or strong someone seems. When a giant named Goliath made everyone afraid, David remembered how God had helped him before and trusted God to help him again.

explorer: What was your favourite part of the story about David today?
David was the smallest in his family, but God chose him because God looks at the heart. What do you think God sees when God looks at {child}'s heart?
Can you say our memory verse, "God looks at the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7), and show me the actions?
trailblazer: David faced a giant because he remembered how God had helped him before. What is one thing that feels like a giant to you right now, and how could you ask God for help with it?
Some giants are not big people. They are the pressure to go along with the crowd when others are being unkind. When might that be hard for you, and who could you talk to?
We learned that David's great-grandmother Ruth came from a different land and still belonged in God's family. Why do you think it matters that God's family includes people from every nation?

mission.title: Brave for a day
mission.description: Do one brave or kind thing this week that you find a bit hard. You could learn how to say a classmate's name properly, or sit with someone who is on their own. Tell a grown-up, and they can confirm it in the app.

familyQuestions: Who do people sometimes pick last? How could we show them that God sees their heart?
Tell about a time you felt like a small person facing a big problem. What helped?

David remembered how God had helped him before. What is one time you remember God helping our family, perhaps in another country or a long time ago? Grandparents and older relatives often have the best stories.

Do you know how your name was chosen? In Ghana many children are named after the day they were born: Kweku for a boy born on a Wednesday, Adjoa for a girl born on a Monday, Kwame for a boy born on a Saturday, Abena for a girl born on a Tuesday. Names from Nigeria and from every other place carry stories too. Ask a grown-up your name's story, and remember that God knows it.
